1. Executive Summary and Macroeconomic Architecture of the Canadian SR&ED Regime

Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program constitutes the single largest federal government initiative supporting business research and development across the country. Administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) alongside fiscal policy oversight from the Department of Finance Canada, the program delivers over $4.6 billion annually in federal investment tax credits (ITCs) across more than 23,677 to 24,160 corporate and unincorporated claimants. While the federal government has provided statutory tax relief for industrial research since 1944, the modern two-pronged architecture of the SR&ED program—combining an immediate, indefinitely carryforwardable income tax deduction pool under Section 37 of the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) with a refundable or non-refundable Investment Tax Credit under Sections 127 and 127.1—was structurally codified between 1985 and 1994. Across Canada, Business Enterprise Research and Development (BERD) is heavily concentrated geographically, with four provinces—Ontario, Québec, British Columbia, and Alberta—historically accounting for approximately 96% to 97% of total national industrial R&D expenditures.

Between 2024 and 2026, the Canadian SR&ED regime underwent its most consequential legislative expansion in over three decades. Following a two-phase national consultation initiated by the Department of Finance Canada in Budget 2024—with the first phase running from January 31, 2024, to April 15, 2024, and the second phase extending until May 27, 2024—the federal government announced sweeping structural reforms in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement, released comprehensive draft legislative amendments in August 2025, and enacted the measures into law through Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Retroactive to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, these reforms doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC from $3 million to $6 million (raising the maximum annual cash refund for qualifying companies from $1.05 million to $2.1 million), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the legacy $10 million–$50 million range to $15 million–$75 million, introduced an elective gross revenue phase-out alternative for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs), extended the 35% enhanced refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and reinstated the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs for property acquired after December 15, 2024. Subsequently, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the elective SR&ED pre-claim approval process announced in Budget 2025 and confirmed in the Spring Economic Update 2026—compressing expenditure review timelines from 180 days to 90 days—and Budget 2026 proposed expanding statutory eligibility to capture key post-R&D commercialisation activities.

Navigating the Canadian R&D tax landscape requires mastering the intricate interplay between federal statutory rules, provincial and territorial top-up credits, and an unforgiving body of Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) jurisprudence. While provincial R&D tax credits are independently administered by Revenu Québec in Québec and by the Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) in Alberta, they are harmonized under CRA administration in Ontario, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon. Provincial credit stacking can elevate total cash recovery on qualifying R&D labour beyond 55% to 74% in jurisdictions such as Québec, Ontario, Alberta, and Atlantic Canada, yet provincial credits simultaneously constitute "government assistance" under Subsection 127(9) and Subsection 127(18) of the Income Tax Act, grinding down the federal qualified expenditure base dollar-for-dollar. Furthermore, because the Federal Court of Appeal has repeatedly affirmed that administrative simplifications by the CRA cannot override the strict five-part common-law test established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, technical documentation and contemporaneous evidence remain the decisive determinants of audit survival.
2. Statutory Foundation and the 2024–2026 Legislative Transformation
2.1 Core Provisions of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

The legal authority governing federal R&D tax incentives resides exclusively within the federal Income Tax Act (ITA) and Part XXIX (Section 2900 et seq.) of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945). Unlike discretionary grant regimes such as the National Research Council's Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), which depend on competitive budget envelopes and prior ministerial approval, the SR&ED program is an entitlement-based statutory mechanism. Any taxpayer carrying on business in Canada that satisfies the technical definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1), incurs eligible expenditures under Section 37 and Section 127, and files the prescribed forms within the mandatory statutory deadline is legally entitled to both the income tax deduction and the investment tax credit. No amount may be claimed as an SR&ED ITC, however, in respect of an expenditure made in the course of earning income if any of the claimant's income is exempt from federal Part I tax under Section 149.

The statutory architecture operates through two distinct but interdependent fiscal mechanisms that separate the deduction of R&D outlays against taxable income from the generation of tax credits against tax payable. The first mechanism is the Subsection 37(1) Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures. Section 37 of the Income Tax Act permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to pool current expenditures under Paragraph 37(1)(a) and—for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024—eligible capital expenditures under restored Paragraph 37(1)(b) incurred in Canada for SR&ED. Even though R&D expenditures generate new scientific knowledge, technology, and intangible assets of an enduring capital nature that would otherwise be barred from current deduction under the general capital prohibition of Paragraph 18(1)(b), Subsection 37(1) allows the claimant to deduct the entire SR&ED expenditure pool against income for tax purposes in the current taxation year or carry any undeducted pool balance forward indefinitely to reduce taxable income in future taxation years. Subsection 37(2) provides a separate, narrower current-year deduction for SR&ED carried on outside Canada, although foreign expenditures (beyond limited permissive salary allowances) do not enter the Subsection 37(1) pool or earn investment tax credits. Subsection 37(8) establishes the interpretive rules governing which expenditures qualify for domestic inclusion under Subsection 37(1) versus foreign inclusion under Subsection 37(2), while Subsection 37(14) imposes a look-through rule to ensure that payments for contract SR&ED or third-party SR&ED reflect eligible underlying expenditures.

The second mechanism is the Sections 127 and 127.1 Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Regime. Subsection 127(5) permits a taxpayer to deduct an Investment Tax Credit from federal Part I tax otherwise payable. Subsection 127(9) defines the core statutory terms, including "investment tax credit," "qualified expenditure," "specified percentage" (setting the 15% basic rate), and "eligible Canadian public corporation". Subsection 127(10.1) provides an additional 20% ITC rate on top of the 15% basic rate—yielding the enhanced 35% ITC rate—for CCPCs and, effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) up to their annual expenditure limit determined under Subsections 127(10.2) through 127(10.62). Section 127.1—specifically Subsections 127.1(1), 127.1(2), and 127.1(2.01)—governs the refundability of unused ITCs, while Subsection 127.1(3) deems any cash refund paid to the taxpayer to have been deducted as an ITC against Part I tax otherwise payable in the year, thereby preventing the refunded credit from being carried back or carried forward.

body.text: 2.2 Enacted Reforms Under Bill C-15 and 2026 Administrative Modernization

The legislative trajectory culminating in Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026) directly addressed structural weaknesses in Canada's innovation ecosystem identified during the 2024 Department of Finance consultations. Prior to these reforms, the federal SR&ED architecture penalised capital-intensive R&D—such as hardware engineering, advanced manufacturing, biotechnology wet labs, clean technology, and sovereign artificial intelligence (AI) compute training—due to the 2012 federal budget repeal of capital expenditure eligibility, which had taken effect after 2013. Furthermore, fast-growing domestic technology firms that listed their shares publicly on a Canadian exchange immediately forfeited CCPC status, suffering an abrupt cliff drop from a 35% fully refundable credit to a 15% non-refundable credit precisely when they required non-dilutive capital to scale in Canada and retain domestic intellectual property.

To rectify these structural distortions, the amendments enacted in Bill C-15—applying retroactively to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (that is, after December 15, 2024)—instituted five core legislative reforms. First, while the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement and initial August 2025 draft explanatory notes originally proposed raising the enhanced expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million, the final enacted framework under Bill C-15 and current CRA administrative policy doubled the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC to $6 million per taxation year. Consequently, the maximum annual refundable federal ITC on current expenditures for a qualifying corporation doubled from $1.05 million to $2.1 million. Second, for CCPCs, the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out range—across which the $6 million expenditure limit is gradually reduced to nil—was widened from the legacy $10 million to $50 million corridor to a substantially broader $15 million to $75 million corridor.

Third, recognising that capital-intensive emerging companies in clean technology, life sciences, and advanced manufacturing frequently accumulate balance-sheet debt or equity capital above $15 million long before generating substantial commercial turnover, Bill C-15 granted CCPCs the option to elect to have their $6 million annual expenditure limit determined and phased out based on their average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years (using the same $15 million to $75 million thresholds) rather than prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada. Fourth, Subsection 127(9) and Subsection 127(10.1) were amended to extend eligibility for the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) on up to $6 million of qualified current expenditures annually, subject to a mandatory three-year average gross revenue phase-out between $15 million and $75 million. Fifth, amendments to Paragraph 37(1)(b), Subsection 127(9), Paragraph 127(11.1)(c.1) (repealed), and Subsection 127.1(2) restored the eligibility of depreciable capital property (such as R&D lab and testing equipment, prototyping machinery, specialized tools, and AI graphics processing units (GPUs)) acquired on or after December 16, 2024, as well as equipment lease costs that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024. Qualifying CCPCs earn a 35% ITC on eligible capital expenditures within their expenditure limit, refundable in cash at a rate of 40%.

In parallel with the statutory enactment of Bill C-15, the Spring Economic Update 2026 and Budget 2026 addressed pivotal administrative and scope modernizations. On the administrative front, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the elective SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval Process first announced in Budget 2025; for claims submitted through this front-loaded technical validation pathway that subsequently require an expenditure review, CRA processing time is reduced from 180 days to 90 days, while standard refundable claim processing targets were accelerated from 60 days to 45 days. On the policy scope front, Budget 2026 proposed a targeted statutory expansion of the SR&ED program to include the costs of key commercialisation activities, addressing long-standing policy goals to retain Canadian intellectual property and help domestic innovators commercialise research outputs within Canada.

body.text: 3. Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Limits, Refundability, and Pool Mechanics
3.1 Basic Versus Enhanced ITC Rate Architecture

The federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit operates on a two-tier rate structure governed by Subsection 127(9) and Subsection 127(10.1) of the Income Tax Act. Under the definition of "specified percentage" in Subsection 127(9), the baseline federal SR&ED ITC rate is 15% of a claimant's total qualified SR&ED expenditures, having been reduced from 20% for taxation years ending after December 31, 2013. This 15% basic rate applies across five distinct claimant and expenditure categories: large domestic public corporations whose three-year average gross revenue exceeds the ECPC phase-out ceiling of $75 million; corporations resident in Canada that are controlled directly or indirectly by one or more non-resident persons (foreign-controlled subsidiaries); private corporations controlled by public corporations (other than eligible subsidiaries within a consolidated ECPC group); CCPCs and ECPCs on the portion of their annual qualified SR&ED expenditures that exceeds their available annual expenditure limit ($6 million maximum, or a lower phased-out limit); and unincorporated claimants, including sole proprietorships (individuals), partners of a partnership (excluding "specified members" who are passive or limited partners statutorily precluded from receiving partnership SR&ED ITC allocations under Subsection 127(8)), and beneficiaries of trusts.

Conversely, under Subsection 127(10.1), a corporation that is throughout the taxation year either a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) as defined in Subsection 125(7) or, for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) as defined in Subsection 127(9), is entitled to add 20% to the 15% basic specified percentage. This statutory addition yields a combined 35% enhanced ITC rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the corporation's annual expenditure limit for the taxation year.
3.2 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas: Taxable Capital Versus Gross Revenue Elections

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit under Subsection 127(10.2) and Subsection 127(10.6) is $6,000,000, prorated under Paragraph 127(10.5)(b) for taxation years of less than 51 weeks based on the number of days in the taxation year divided by 365, and shared among associated corporations via T2 Schedule 49 under Subsection 127(10.3). Prior to March 19, 2019, a CCPC's expenditure limit was subject to a dual phase-out based on both prior-year taxable income (phasing out between $500,000 and $800,000) and prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (phasing out between $10 million and $50 million). Budget 2019 repealed the taxable income factor for taxation years ending on or after March 19, 2019, leaving taxable capital as the sole phase-out metric until the enactment of Bill C-15. Under the current post-December 15, 2024 statutory framework, a CCPC's $6,000,000 expenditure limit is determined using either the default Taxable Capital Method or the elective Gross Revenue Method:
Expressed in standard linear reduction terms for a phase-out metric falling within the corridor of $15,000,000 to $75,000,000, the formula operates as follows:

Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is nil if the phase-out metric is $15,000,000 or less and otherwise equals the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which the phase-out metric exceeds $15,000,000.

Under the default Taxable Capital Method available to CCPCs, the variable A represents the aggregate taxable capital employed in Canada (within the meaning of Part I.3 of the Income Tax Act) of the CCPC and all associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year. Every $10 of prior-year taxable capital in excess of $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1, until the enhanced expenditure limit is completely eliminated at $75,000,000 of taxable capital. Under the Gross Revenue Method—which is elective for CCPCs under Subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) and mandatory for ECPCs under Subsection 127(10.6)—the variable A represents the average annual gross revenue of the corporation and all members of its associated CCPC group or consolidated ECPC group over the three preceding fiscal years, as reflected in their financial statements. To calculate average annual revenues for the three preceding fiscal years, the Income Tax Act requires aggregating the financial statement revenues for each corporation or entity (where "entity" is defined in Subsection 127(9) for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, to include any corporation, partnership, trust, or other registered or unregistered arrangement for which separate financial accounts are prepared) that is a member of the group in the current taxation year, across the preceding three fiscal years, regardless of whether those entities were associated during the entirety of that lookback period. The legislation permits reasonable adjustments, such as eliminating intra-group sales of goods or services, so that the annual revenue of the group accurately reflects that of a single economic entity. Where a corporation or group has fewer than three preceding fiscal years, the average annual revenue is computed over the actual number of completed fiscal years (one or two fiscal years).

For taxation years that began before December 16, 2024, the legacy formula applies strictly to CCPCs based on prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada: Expenditure Limit = $3,000,000 × ($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000, where A is the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $10,000,000.

Specific statutory rules under Paragraph 127(10.5)(a) (for CCPCs) and Paragraph 127(10.64)(a) (for ECPCs) apply to determine the expenditure limit if a CCPC or ECPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year and is associated in two or more of those taxation years with another CCPC or ECPC that has a taxation year ending in that same calendar year. Furthermore, under the anti-avoidance provision of Subsection 256(2.1), two or more corporations are deemed to be associated with each other if one of the main reasons for the separate existence of those corporations in a taxation year is to reduce the amount of tax otherwise payable or to increase the amount of any refund of tax under the Income Tax Act. Conversely, the relieving provisions of Subsections 127(10.22) and 127.1(2.2) (subject to Subsections 127(10.23) and 127.1(2.3)) ensure that CCPCs that would be considered associated solely because of the extended definition of a "group of persons" in Paragraph 256(1.2)(a) (such as unrelated portfolio companies backed by the same venture capital syndicates) are not treated as associated for calculating the refundable ITC or determining the expenditure limit, provided that at least one shareholder of one of the corporations is not a shareholder of the other corporation and that the existence of such distinct shareholdings is not designed merely to satisfy the relieving provision.
3.3 Extension to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations

The creation of the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) category under Subsection 127(9) and Subsections 127(10.6) to 127(10.62) eliminates a major disincentive to domestic public listings in Canada. To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year beginning on or after December 16, 2024, a corporation must be resident in Canada throughout the taxation year, must be a public corporation (or an "eligible subsidiary" of such a public corporation within a consolidated group, as newly defined in Subsection 127(9)), and must not be controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons.

While ECPCs earn the same 35% enhanced rate (100% refundable on current expenditures) up to the $6 million expenditure limit as CCPCs, two fundamental statutory distinctions separate ECPCs from CCPCs. First, unlike CCPCs, an ECPC cannot determine its expenditure limit using prior-year taxable capital; its $6 million annual expenditure limit is phased out strictly between $15 million and $75 million of average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years (shared across members of a consolidated ECPC group under Subsection 127(10.62)). Second, for an ECPC, qualifying SR&ED expenditures in excess of its annual expenditure limit earn the basic 15% ITC on a strictly non-refundable basis; unlike qualifying CCPCs, ECPCs are statutorily barred from claiming the 40% partial refundability on expenditures exceeding their annual expenditure limit.
3.4 Refundability Matrix, Carryover Horizons, Pool Taxation, and Recapture Rules

Section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act governs the conversion of unused SR&ED ITCs into cash refunds. A claimant's entitlement to cash refundability depends on whether it is a "qualifying corporation" as defined in Subsection 127.1(2) (a CCPC whose prior-year taxable income, combined with that of its associated corporations, does not exceed its qualifying income limit of $500,000, which is phased out between $15 million and $75 million of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada), a CCPC within the phase-out corridor governed by Subsection 127.1(2.01) (a CCPC that is neither a qualifying corporation nor an excluded corporation), an ECPC, an unincorporated individual or trust, or a non-qualifying corporation.

body.text: Unused non-refundable SR&ED ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable in those preceding years (after taking into account any ITCs already refunded in those prior years) and carried forward up to 20 taxation years under Subsection 127(5) and Subsection 127(9). Under Subsection 127.1(3), any SR&ED ITC that is refunded in cash during a taxation year is deemed to have been applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable in that year, directly reducing the balance of ITCs available for carryback or carryforward. Moreover, if a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control, the amount by which it may carry back unused ITCs earned after the acquisition of control—or carry forward unused ITCs earned prior to the acquisition of control—is strictly restricted to offsetting Part I tax derived from carrying on the same or a similar business.

A foundational accounting and tax mechanic of the Canadian regime is that SR&ED tax credits are themselves subject to tax inclusion through pool reductions. For federal ITCs, any credit claimed to reduce Part I tax payable or received as a cash refund in a given taxation year must be deducted from the Subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the immediately following taxation year, reported on Line 435 of Form T661. If that prior-year federal ITC exceeds the current year's Subsection 37(1) pool balance, the resulting negative pool balance is brought into the taxpayer's taxable income in the following year, providing a one-year tax deferral on the federal credit. By contrast, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" under Subsection 127(9). Consequently, under Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsection 127(18), any provincial R&D tax credit earned in a taxation year reduces both the Subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool and the Section 127 federal qualified SR&ED expenditure base in the current taxation year, unless the claimant formally renounces a non-refundable provincial credit on or before its income tax return filing due date.

Finally, under Subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Income Tax Act, the recapture period for SR&ED ITCs is 20 years. If a corporation acquires property (including capital equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, shared-use equipment, or materials transformed into a prototype) on which an SR&ED ITC was earned, and within 20 years disposes of the property or converts it to commercial use, the taxpayer must report a recapture of the ITC in Parts 16, 17, and 24 of T2 Schedule 31. The recaptured amount is added directly to federal Part I tax payable and equals the lesser of the original ITC earned on the property or the amount determined by applying the percentage used in calculating the original ITC (35% or 15%) to the proceeds of disposition (if disposed of to an arm's-length person) or to the fair market value of the property (in any non-arm's-length disposition or conversion to commercial use). Where the disposition or conversion occurs within a partnership, Subsection 127(28) reduces the partnership ITC allocated to the members by the amount of the recapture.
4. Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures and Overhead Allocation Methodologies

To earn an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit, an outlay must constitute a "qualified expenditure" under Subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act. Qualified expenditures are calculated across Part 3 (Lines 300 to 470) and Part 4 (Lines 500 to 570) of Form T661. Under Subsection 78(4) and the CRA's expenditure policies, both current expenditures and salary or wages incurred in a taxation year must be actually paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year; any expenditure remaining unpaid after 180 days from year-end is excluded from the current year's SR&ED claim (deducted on Line 520 of Form T661 for unpaid current expenditures) and only becomes eligible in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid.
4.1 Direct Salaries, Wages, and Specified Employee Restrictions

Salaries and wages of employees working in Canada represent the primary expenditure category in Canadian SR&ED claims, with Canadian businesses spending over $20.7 billion annually on in-house R&D wages. To qualify on Line 300 (for regular employees) or Line 305 (for specified employees) of Form T661, the remuneration must be paid to T4 employees of the claimant who are "directly engaged in SR&ED". For income tax purposes, a partner cannot be an employee of a partnership, and drawings or salaries paid to sole proprietors or partners are distributions of income that cannot be claimed as SR&ED salary or wages. Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, whether an employee is directly engaged in SR&ED is governed strictly by the hands-on technical tasks performed rather than the employee's corporate job title. Eligible duties encompass hands-on scientific experimentation, prototype fabrication, software coding, mathematical analysis, commensurate support work across the eight statutory categories of Paragraph 248(1)(d), and direct first-line technological supervision of experimental staff, whereas general administrative management and executive oversight are excluded unless directly tied to hands-on project execution.

Eligible salary or wages include base salary, overtime, vacation pay, and the employer's share of direct statutory payroll levies (such as Canada Pension Plan, Québec Pension Plan, Employment Insurance, and workers' compensation). Conversely, non-taxable benefits (such as employer contributions to private health plans or pension plans) do not form part of salary or wages on Line 300, though they may be claimed as incremental overhead on Line 360 if the taxpayer elects the Traditional Method.

Special statutory anti-avoidance restrictions apply to "specified employees"—defined in Subsection 248(1) as employees who are specified shareholders owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation, or who do not deal at arm's length with the corporation. First, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits paid to specified employees are completely prohibited from SR&ED eligibility, and even for non-specified employees, bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and taxable benefits included on Line 810 must be stripped out on Line 812 when computing the salary base for the Prescribed Proxy Amount. Second, the total eligible SR&ED salary of a specified employee included in the Subsection 37(1) pool and Section 127 ITC base is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) under the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days employed in the taxation year and allocated among associated corporations using Form T1174. Third, when calculating the salary base for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount in Part 5 of Form T661, each specified employee's includable salary is restricted to the lesser of 75% of the employee's total salary or wages (excluding bonuses and taxable benefits) for the year, and 2.5 times the YMPE prorated by days of employment.
4.2 Materials Consumed or Transformed and Cloud Computing Infrastructure

Under Subparagraph 37(8)(a)(ii) and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, claimants may include 100% of the cost of materials consumed or materials transformed in performing SR&ED in Canada. Materials consumed are physical inputs rendered virtually worthless or destroyed during experimental trials, whereas materials transformed (eligible since February 23, 1998) are components integrated into experimental prototypes or pilot plants during SR&ED. Materials that are resold or incorporated directly into commercial production without experimental transformation do not qualify, and any transformed prototype that is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years triggers ITC recapture under Subsection 127(27).

For software engineering, SaaS, and artificial intelligence claimants, cloud computing costs (such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP)) represent a critical expenditure category. Under CRA audit guidelines and industry practice, cloud computing costs used specifically for R&D experimentation—such as novel model architecture training, staging, and experimental testing environments—are eligible to be claimed (frequently categorized under materials consumed or directly related R&D infrastructure), whereas cloud infrastructure supporting commercial production workloads or customer hosting is strictly ineligible. Claimants must maintain separate cloud billing accounts or granular resource-tagging ledgers that segregate R&D development environments from commercial production infrastructure. Furthermore, under the post-December 15, 2024 legislative reforms enacted in Bill C-15, fees for software and cloud space used for development, along with purchased or leased AI/ML GPUs and dedicated experimental servers, are explicitly recognized within the expanded SR&ED expenditure framework.
4.3 Arm's-Length Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Transfers, and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant contracts external parties to perform SR&ED in Canada on its behalf (reported on Line 340 of Form T661), 100% of the contract expenditure paid to an arm's-length "taxable supplier" (a Canadian resident individual, corporation, or Canadian permanent establishment) is deductible in the Subsection 37(1) pool. For Investment Tax Credit purposes under Subsection 127(9), however, only 80% of arm's-length contract expenditures are eligible to earn the 35% or 15% ITC—a statutory restriction effective after 2012 that requires subtracting 20% of Line 340 and Line 370 expenditures on Line 529 of Form T661. Under the Subsection 37(14) look-through rule, only the technical SR&ED portion of a Canadian contractor's invoice qualifies, and any amount paid in respect of an SR&ED contract to a foreign person or partnership that is not a taxable supplier in Canada is completely disallowed for ITC purposes on Line 528. Moreover, contractor expenditures never form part of the salary base for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount.

Where SR&ED is performed by a non-arm's-length contractor, the contract payments themselves do not earn an ITC in the hands of the payer. Instead, the non-arm's-length parties may execute Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer the performer's underlying qualified SR&ED expenditures to the payer (reported by the performer on Line 540 of Form T661). Separate rules govern third-party payments (Line 370 of Form T661), which are payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit R&D associations in Canada for SR&ED related to the claimant's business. Like arm's-length subcontracts, third-party payments are 100% deductible under Subsection 37(1) and 80% eligible for the federal ITC (subject to the 20% reduction on Line 529), and require filing Form T1263.
4.4 Reinstated Capital Expenditures, Equipment Leases, and Shared-Use Equipment

Reversing the policy repeal that had barred capital assets since 2014, Bill C-15 reinstated the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs for depreciable property acquired (and available for use) after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024), and for lease costs that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024. Capital expenditures made or property acquired before December 16, 2024, remain strictly ineligible.

Under the restored rules, an SR&ED capital expenditure (reported on Line 390 of Form T661, including both new and used depreciable equipment) is an outlay to acquire depreciable property that the claimant intended at the time of acquisition either to use all or substantially all (ASA)—defined by the CRA as 90% or more—of its operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or to consume ASA (90% or more) of its value to perform SR&ED in Canada. Eligible capital assets include R&D laboratory and testing apparatus, prototyping machinery, specialized tools and devices, infrastructure used for experimentation, and hardware-intensive AI/ML compute such as GPUs. Conversely, non-depreciable assets (such as land), buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are statutorily excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures. Capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 are deducted in the Subsection 37(1) pool under Paragraph 37(1)(b) and must not be included on T2 Schedule 8 for regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) depreciation. For qualifying CCPCs, the 35% enhanced ITC earned on eligible capital expenditures is refundable at a rate of 40% under Subsection 127.1(2).

If newly acquired depreciable equipment does not meet the 90% ASA threshold, it may still qualify for SR&ED ITCs as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Line 504 of Form T661 if it is used primarily (more than 50% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada. Under the SUE regime—which operates identically under both the Proxy and Traditional overhead methods—the capital cost of the equipment is not included in the Subsection 37(1) deductible pool and is instead depreciated under regular CCA rules on T2 Schedule 8. For ITC purposes on Line 504, the claimant includes 25% of the capital cost of the equipment in the first period (first-term SUE) and another 25% in the second period (second-term SUE), provided the equipment meets the primary SR&ED operating-time test in each respective period. Lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for SR&ED equipment are similarly restored to eligibility.
4.5 Overhead Methodologies: Prescribed Proxy Amount Versus Traditional Method

In Part 3, Section A of Form T661, a claimant must make an irrevocable annual election for the taxation year between the Proxy Method (Line 160) and the Traditional Method (Line 162) to account for SR&ED overhead and other expenditures. Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not specifically track or itemise overhead expenses on Line 360 (which is entered as zero); instead, the claimant computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5, Section B (Line 820) equal to 55% of the eligible salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED. Because the PPA is a notional calculation, it is never added to the Subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool—actual underlying overhead expenses are simply deducted as ordinary business expenses—but the 55% PPA is added to qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 502 of Part 4 to earn the 35% or 15% SR&ED ITC (including 100% cash refundability for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs). The PPA covers and precludes separately claiming office supplies, general-purpose office equipment, utilities (heat, water, electricity, and telephones), support staff salaries, travel and training, property taxes, maintenance and upkeep of SR&ED premises or equipment, and any other incremental expenditure directly related to SR&ED.

Under the Traditional Method (Line 162), the claimant foregoes the 55% PPA and instead specifically identifies, tracks, and allocates actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 that are directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED and incremental (meaning they would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not been carried out). Traditional overhead includes incremental utilities, facility maintenance, travel, training, non-taxable employee benefits, and contract costs for non-SR&ED support trades (such as electricians, welders, and mechanics) directly and incrementally supporting SR&ED work.

body.text: 4.6 Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Contract Payment Grind-Downs

Under Subsections 127(18) to 127(20) and Paragraph 37(1)(d) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must reduce its Subsection 37(1) pool and its Section 127 qualified SR&ED expenditures by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive. Government assistance encompasses grants, subsidies, forgivable loans, and provincial or territorial R&D tax credits. In CCLC Technologies Inc. v. The Queen (96 D.T.C. 6527) and CAE Inc. v. The Queen (2022 FCA 178), the Federal Court of Appeal held that government payments or conditionally repayable loans not provided in the ordinary course of commercial business to advance the business interests of the payer constituted government assistance. However, effective January 1, 2020 (for loans made after December 31, 2019), the definition of government assistance was amended to carve out an "excluded loan" newly defined in Subsection 12(11) of the Income Tax Act, preventing qualifying repayable government innovation loans from grinding down SR&ED claims.

Non-government assistance (reported on Line 517 of Form T661) includes inducements, reimbursements, grants, or allowances received from private entities. Contract payments (also deducted on Line 517) are amounts paid or payable to a claimant by an arm's-length taxable supplier—or by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or tax-exempt entity under Section 149—for SR&ED to be performed for it or on its behalf. When a contractor performs SR&ED on behalf of a Canadian client, the contractor must reduce its qualified expenditures by the contract payment received or receivable. When the aggregate assistance and contract payments relating to a project exceed the SR&ED expenditures of that project, Subsection 127(19) reduces the qualified expenditures of the claimant and any non-arm's-length party to nil, and unapplied assistance may be allocated among non-arm's-length parties using Form T1145. Conversely, if a claimant subsequently repays government or non-government assistance that previously reduced its SR&ED pool or qualified expenditures, the repayment increases the deductible pool on Line 445 and adds back to qualified expenditures on Line 560 in the year of repayment.
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Incentive Regimes

In addition to the federal SR&ED program, eight Canadian provinces and one territory offer statutory R&D tax credits. While Ontario, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon harmonize their technical eligibility with Subsection 248(1) of the federal Income Tax Act and are administered by the CRA via schedules filed with the T2 return, Québec and Alberta administer their R&D tax incentives independently through separate provincial tax returns.
5.1 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Administered by the CRA since 2009, Ontario provides three distinct corporate R&D tax credits that may be stacked concurrently on eligible expenditures incurred through a permanent establishment in Ontario. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on T2 Schedule 566, is an 8% refundable tax credit (reduced from 10% for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016) available to qualifying CCPCs on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures per taxation year, yielding up to $240,000 in annual cash refunds. Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on T2 Schedule 508, is a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit available to all corporations performing SR&ED in Ontario with no expenditure limit, calculated on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures net of any OITC or OBRITC claimed. Unused ORDTC credits may be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years, or formally renounced by the income tax filing due date so they do not grind down the federal SR&ED expenditure pool and ITC base under Subsection 127(18). Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), claimed on T2 Schedule 569 (alongside Schedule 568), provides a 20% refundable tax credit on qualified payments made under eligible research contracts with approved Ontario universities, colleges, or research institutes, up to an annual expenditure cap of $20,000,000.
5.2 Québec: Revenu Québec Administration and Specialized Refundable Credits

Québec's R&D tax credits are administered independently by Revenu Québec and must be claimed with the Québec provincial income tax return (CO-17 for corporations or TP-1 for individuals/partnerships), accompanied by Form RD-222-V (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures) and guided by Revenu Québec Publication IN-109-V (Tax Assistance for Scientific Research and Experimental Development). Unlike the federal regime, Québec does not use the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount for overhead and excludes specified members of partnerships, tax-exempt trusts, and Crown-controlled corporations from claiming R&D tax credits.

Under its established four-credit structure, Revenu Québec provides: (1) the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D), claimed on Form RD-1029.7-V (with associated corporations allocating the $3,000,000 expenditure limit via Form RD-1029.7.8-T), offering a refundable credit of up to 30% for SMEs (phasing down to a 14% basic refundable rate for large corporations) on Québec R&D salaries and 50% of arm's-length Québec subcontractor fees above a statutory exclusion threshold; (2) the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium, claimed on Form RD-1029.8.6-V for eligible contracts with Québec universities, public research centres, or research consortia; (3) the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research, claimed on Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V and requiring a qualification certificate issued by the Minister of Economy, Innovation and Energy (MEIE); and (4) the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium, claimed on Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V. In addition, as noted on Revenu Québec's R&D portal and the 2025-09 version of Form RD-1029.7-V, Québec introduced a consolidated New Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (the CRIC regime) for fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, unifying the legacy credits and expanding support to pre-commercialisation and capital expenditures.
5.3 Alberta: Innovation Employment Grant Base and Incremental Architecture

Administered independently by the Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) under Division 7 of Part 6 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and detailed in Information Circular IEG-1R5 (and the Guide to Claiming the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant, updated June 2026), the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) is a refundable tax credit available for taxation years ending after December 31, 2020. To claim the IEG, a qualified corporation must file AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) and Form AT4970 (Listing of SR&ED / Innovation Employment Grant Projects Carried Out in Alberta) with its Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return (Form AT1, reported on Line 129) within the mandatory filing deadline of 18 months after the end of the taxation year. If Schedule 29 is filed past the deadline, TRA rejects the claim by letter without issuing an assessment. Furthermore, TRA only determines and disburses a corporation's IEG after receiving confirmation from the CRA of the corporation's federal SR&ED expenditures reported on Line 559 of federal Form T661.

The IEG provides an 8% base refundable credit on the lesser of the corporation's eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures and its maximum expenditure limit of $4,000,000, plus an additional 12% incremental refundable credit (yielding a combined 20% refundable rate) on the amount by which the corporation's eligible Alberta expenditures (up to the $4,000,000 maximum limit) exceed its "base amount":
IEG = (8% × lesser of eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures and $4,000,000) + (12% × the amount by which eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures, up to $4,000,000, exceed the base amount)

The base amount is calculated as the average of the corporation's eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures (from Line 559 of federal Form T661) over the two immediately preceding taxation years. If a corporation had no eligible Alberta expenditures in the preceding two years, its base amount is nil ($0), entitling it to the full 20% refundable rate on up to $4,000,000 of expenditures (up to $800,000 in cash). Recapture rules under the Alberta Corporate Tax Act claw back the proportionate IEG if property on which an IEG was received is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use.
5.4 British Columbia, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba

In British Columbia, the BC SR&ED Tax Credit—governed by Part 6 (Sections 97 to 102.6) of the British Columbia Income Tax Act and administered by the CRA—is now permanent. Qualifying CCPCs with a permanent establishment in BC earn a 10% refundable tax credit up to their annual expenditure limit ($3,000,000, claimed on Line 674 of Schedule 5), while non-CCPCs and CCPCs with BC expenditures exceeding their expenditure limit earn a 10% non-refundable tax credit (claimed on Line 659 of Schedule 5, with a 3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward, or optional renunciation under Subsection 100(1) of the BC Act). Corporations must file Form T666 with their T2 return no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year; individuals are ineligible, and a 10-year recapture rule applies on Line 241 of Schedule 5 if BC SR&ED property is disposed of or converted to commercial use.

In Saskatchewan, Sections 63 to 63.4 of The Income Tax Act, 2000 (Saskatchewan) provide a 10% R&D tax credit administered by the CRA on T2 Schedule 403 (T2SCH403). The credit is refundable for qualifying CCPCs on the first $1,000,000 of eligible Saskatchewan SR&ED expenditures and non-refundable on remaining eligible expenditures (with a 3-year carryback, 10-year carryforward, no recapture, and an option to renounce non-refundable credits prior to the federal Paragraph 37(1)(d) / Subsection 127(18) reduction date).

In Manitoba, Section 7.3 of The Income Tax Act (Manitoba) provides a 15% R&D tax credit (reduced from 20% for expenditures made after April 11, 2017) administered by the CRA on T2 Schedule 380 (T2SCH380), which must be filed within 1 year after the T2 filing due date (18 months after year-end). For in-house R&D carried out in Manitoba, one-half of the credit (7.5%) is refundable and the other half (7.5%) is non-refundable (with a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward), whereas R&D performed under contract with an eligible educational institution is fully refundable. No recapture applies in Manitoba, and a corporation may renounce non-refundable Manitoba credits on or before 6 months after its tax year-end for federal purposes.
5.5 Atlantic Canada and Yukon

The provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Newfoundland and Labrador, along with the Yukon Territory, offer uncapped 15% fully refundable R&D tax credits administered by the CRA to corporations with a permanent establishment in the respective jurisdiction. Nova Scotia provides a 15% refundable credit claimed on T2 Schedule 340, New Brunswick provides a 15% refundable credit claimed on T2 Schedule 360, Newfoundland and Labrador provides a 15% refundable credit claimed on T2 Schedule 301, and Yukon provides a 15% refundable credit (increasing to 20% on payments to Yukon University) for both corporations and individuals. Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not maintain territorial or provincial R&D income tax credit programs.

body.text: 5.7 Integrated Federal-Provincial Stacking Calculation Model

Because provincial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" under Subsection 127(18) of the Income Tax Act, they reduce the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure base before the 35% (or 15%) federal ITC rate is applied. However, when an R&D performer elects the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) on direct T4 salaries, the 1.55 proxy multiplier expands the qualified expenditure base prior to the provincial grind-down, producing an effective cash recovery on direct R&D labour that substantially exceeds the headline statutory rate.

For a qualifying CCPC incurring $1,000,000 of direct T4 SR&ED salaries in Ontario and electing the 55% proxy method (a gross proxy base of $1,550,000), after claiming the 8% refundable OITC ($1,550,000 × 8% = $124,000) and the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC on the net base ($1,426,000 × 3.5% = $49,910), total Ontario credits equal $173,910, leaving a net federal qualified base of $1,376,090, which earns a 35% federal refundable ITC of $481,632, for a combined tax credit recovery of $655,542 (65.55%). Renouncing the ORDTC removes $49,910 from the grind-down (leaving a net federal base of $1,426,000), increasing the 35% federal cash refund to $499,100 and yielding $623,100 (62.31%) in pure immediate cash.

body.text: 6. Technological Eligibility Criteria and Binding Canadian Jurisprudence
6.1 Statutory Definition Under Subsection 248(1): Eligible Categories, Support Work, and Exclusions

Work is eligible for SR&ED tax incentives only when it satisfies the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls within one of three core categories: (a) basic research, namely work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; (b) applied research, namely work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; or (c) experimental development, namely work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

In addition to direct basic research, applied research, and experimental development, Paragraph 248(1)(d) includes "support work" undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustive statutory disciplines—engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Conversely, Paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) explicitly exclude seven categories of commercial and routine activities from the meaning of SR&ED: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; and (k) routine data collection. As the CRA's eligibility guidelines explain, distinguishing between eligible support work under Paragraph 248(1)(d) (such as data collection or testing) and excluded work under Paragraphs 248(1)(f) or (k) turns on the underlying purpose of the activity: if data collection or testing is carried out specifically and directly to support experimental development aimed at resolving a technological uncertainty, it qualifies as support work, whereas data collection performed for standard commercial or operational reasons is excluded.
6.2 The CRA's 2021 "Why and How" Administrative Guidelines Versus Judicial Precedent

On August 13, 2021, the CRA replaced its 2015 Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (which had explicitly organized project reviews around five sequential questions) with the consolidated Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. The 2021 Guidelines present two overarching requirements—the "Why" and the "How"—both of which are derived from Subsection 248(1) and must be met for work to qualify.

The "Why" requirement asks why the work was conducted: it must be conducted for the purpose of advancing scientific knowledge or achieving a technological advancement by resolving a scientific or technological uncertainty. Indicators that existing technological knowledge is insufficient include situations where existing design methods are inapplicable, requirements or specifications conflict with existing standards, too many variables or unknowns interact unpredictably, or operating parameters lie outside normal ranges. Acquiring existing knowledge through training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants, or purchasing proprietary technology does not satisfy the requirement of attempting to achieve technological advancement. The "How" requirement asks how the work was conducted: it must be carried out by means of a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Fulfilling the "How" requirement involves four connected steps: generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts as a starting point for resolving the problem; testing that idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis (allowing the hypothesis to evolve as testing progresses); developing logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis; and keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.

Crucially, following the publication of the 2021 Guidelines, taxpayers in appellate litigation argued that the CRA's simplified "Why and How" terminology eliminated the common-law requirement to follow the scientific method. In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen (2021 FCA 88) and National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72), the Federal Court of Appeal firmly rejected that argument, holding that it is the constitutional role of the courts to interpret the Income Tax Act and that the CRA's 2021 administrative guidelines neither removed the requirement to follow the scientific method nor altered the binding five-part judicial test established in Northwest Hydraulic.
6.3 The Landmark Five-Part Legal Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen

The cornerstone judicial authority governing SR&ED eligibility in Canada is Justice Donald Bowman's decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (Tax Court of Canada). At paragraph 16 of Northwest Hydraulic, Justice Bowman established five cumulative criteria—all five of which must be answered in the affirmative—to determine whether a particular project constitutes SR&ED under Subsection 248(1) and Regulation 2900.

First, was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? If the resolution of a problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures or routine engineering known to competent professionals in the field, no technological uncertainty exists. Second, did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? Third, did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? Fourth, did the process result in a scientific or technological advancement—that is, an advancement in the stock of technological knowledge, even if a hypothesis is ultimately rejected or the project fails commercially? Fifth, was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?
6.4 Appellate and Tax Court Jurisprudence on Scientific Method, Uncertainty, and Documentation

The Northwest Hydraulic five-question test was explicitly endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 D.T.C. 5087), C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393), Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 FCA 355), Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen (2021 FCA 88), and National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72). The following table synthesizes the controlling Canadian case law governing SR&ED audits and litigation.

Distinction between trial-and-error engineering and systematic scientific investigation.

Confirmed that all five Northwest Hydraulic questions must be answered in the affirmative; resolving engineering hurdles through unguided trial-and-error without formulating and testing causal hypotheses fails Criteria 2 and 3.
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6
Custom mechanical rigging systems and motorized stage winches.

Clarified Criterion 2 (hypothesis formulation) and Criterion 1 (technological uncertainty), emphasizing that designing custom mechanical components using established engineering principles does not constitute SR&ED.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88 (Docket A-442-19)
Whether Criterion 3 ("scientific method") is legally required if the words "scientific method" do not appear in s. 248(1).

Dismissed the taxpayer's appeal for its 2009–2010 SR&ED claims. Held that Justice Bowman's third criterion (scientific method) is the authoritative judicial interpretation of "systematic investigation or search ... by means of experiment or analysis" in s. 248(1).
National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47)
Impact of the CRA's 2021 SR&ED Guidelines on the scientific method requirement; admissibility of expert witness reports.

Dismissed the software consulting firm's appeal. Held that (1) the CRA's 2021 Guidelines did not remove the requirement to follow the scientific method; (2) vague, unclear records that do not show a logical progression between premise and result fail Criteria 3 and 5; and (3) expert reports opining on the ultimate legal question are inadmissible.
CAE Inc. v. The Queen, 2022 FCA 178 (aff'g 2021 TCC 57)
Whether low-interest, conditionally repayable government R&D loans constitute "government assistance" under s. 127(9) and s. 127(18).

Held that pre-2020 government R&D loans provided on non-commercial terms constituted "government assistance" that reduced qualified SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar (subsequently addressed for post-2019 loans by the "excluded loan" carve-out in s. 12(11)).
Food science formulation and industrial baking process parameters.

Upheld the taxpayer's SR&ED tax credits, confirming that systematic testing of interacting variables in an applied commercial environment satisfies the Northwest Hydraulic and Joel Theatrical standards.

body.text: 7. Governance, Filing Procedures, Prescribed Forms, and Audit Defence Protocols
7.1 Governing Authorities, Statutory Filing Deadlines, and the Zero-Discretion Rule

The federal SR&ED program is jointly governed by the Department of Finance Canada (which formulates legislative tax policy) and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) (which administers claims through its network of SR&ED Coordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs) and tax centres). Under Subsections 37(11) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, a claimant must file the prescribed forms (Form T661 alongside T2 Schedule 31 for corporations or Form T2038(IND) for individuals) containing the prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year.

Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year, the corporate SR&ED reporting deadline is strictly 18 months after the end of the taxation year (for example, a corporation with a December 31, 2024 taxation year-end must file its complete SR&ED claim on or before June 30, 2026). When the claimant is a partnership, the partnership cannot carry forward a Subsection 37(1) expenditure pool and must deduct SR&ED expenditures in full at the partnership level while allocating the resulting SR&ED ITC to active non-specified partners under Subsection 127(8). Where a partnership's members are a combination of individuals (including trusts) and corporations, its filing due date is the earlier of March 31 after the calendar year in which the fiscal period ended or 5 months after the end of the partnership's fiscal period.

The 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline is an absolute statutory bar with zero ministerial discretion for late-filing relief. Submitting a letter expressing an "intent to file" an SR&ED claim does not satisfy the statutory filing requirements, and if a claimant fails to file Form T661 and Schedule 31 containing the prescribed project and expenditure information by the 18-month deadline, the claimant is legally barred from deducting any SR&ED expenditures in the Subsection 37(1) pool or earning any SR&ED ITC for that taxation year.
7.2 Architecture of Form T661, Part 2 Technical Narratives, and Part 9 Preparer Penalties

Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, explained in CRA Guide T4088) is divided into ten parts. Part 1 captures general corporate information. Part 2 (Sections A to C) captures the technical project information on a project-by-project basis and should be prepared by technical personnel familiar with the scientific or technological content of the work. While a claimant filing more than 20 projects may elect to submit Part 2 descriptions for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value at the time of filing, the cost of every project must be included in Part 6 at filing, and the claimant must complete and maintain at its place of business a full Part 2 for every project claimed, ready to submit upon CRA request under pain of immediate disallowance. Section B of Part 2 requires narrative descriptions of the scientific or technological uncertainties attempted to be overcome (Line 242), the systematic work performed in chronological order—detailing the hypotheses formulated, experiments or analyses conducted, results obtained, and conclusions drawn (Line 244)—and the scientific or technological advancements achieved or attempted.

Part 3 (Sections A to C) records the irrevocable overhead method election (Line 160 for Proxy vs. Line 162 for Traditional), calculates current and capital SR&ED expenditures, and determines the Subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool. Notably, while identifying expenditures into the pool is subject to the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline, the decision to deduct an amount from an already-identified pool balance is not subject to the 18-month deadline. Part 4 calculates qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes (Lines 500 to 570), Part 5 computes the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Lines 810 to 820), Part 6 allocates project-by-project costs, Part 7 collects statistical data, and Part 8 provides a claim checklist.

Part 9 (Claim Preparer Information) mandates complete disclosure for every external claim preparer who has accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the SR&ED claim, including their billing arrangement (such as contingency fees, which typically range from 15% to 25% in the market, or flat-fee arrangements). While missing or incomplete information in Part 9 will not invalidate the SR&ED claim itself and is not subject to the 18-month reporting deadline, a $1,000 penalty may be assessed if the prescribed information regarding the claim preparer(s) and billing arrangement(s) is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable. Part 10 contains the mandatory certification signed by an authorized signing officer of the corporation, who remains legally responsible for filing a compliant claim even if misled by third-party promotions.

body.text: 7.4 CRA Review Mechanics, Pre-Claim Approval, and Gross Negligence Penalties

To assist claimants in preparing compliant submissions, the CRA provides the Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT) and the secure SR&ED Client Portal within My Business Account. While historically around 91% of SR&ED claims were accepted as filed or with minor modifications and processed under a 60-day service standard for refundable claims (or 180 days for audited claims), the 2026 administrative modernization accelerated refundable claim processing targets to 45 days and launched the elective SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval Process, which reduces expenditure review processing times from 180 days to 90 days.

Where a claimant files an overstated SR&ED claim containing a false statement or omission made knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence—whether in an initial income tax return or an amended return—the CRA may assess a severe penalty under its Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy and Paragraphs 163(2)(a) and 163(2)(d) of the Income Tax Act. To impose the penalty, the CRA bears the burden of showing on a balance of probabilities that the false statement or omission resulted from more than a simple oversight or misunderstanding of the Income Tax Act. The gross negligence penalty equals the greater of $100 and 50% of the sum of: (1) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission under Paragraph 163(2)(a) (taking into account multi-year pool overstatements reduced by subsequent-year ITC pool deductions); plus (2) the refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed by the claimant under Paragraph 163(2)(d).
8. Strategic Conclusions and Compliance Recommendations for Canadian Claimants

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026—retroactive to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024—together with the 2026 Pre-Claim Approval launch and proposed commercialisation expansions, marks a generational strengthening of Canada's R&D tax incentive architecture. By doubling the 35% enhanced expenditure limit from $3 million to $6 million (delivering up to $2.1 million annually in federal cash refunds), widening the phase-out thresholds to $15 million–$75 million, introducing the three-year average gross revenue election for CCPCs, extending the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restoring the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs, Parliament has significantly enhanced non-dilutive funding for Canadian innovators.

To maximise recovery while mitigating audit and penalty exposure under this modernized regime, Canadian enterprises should embed five operational practices into their tax and engineering governance. First, capital-intensive CCPCs whose prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15 million due to venture debt or equity financings—but whose three-year average gross revenue remains below $15 million—should formally elect the gross revenue phase-out method under Subsection 127(10.31) or 127(10.32) to preserve their full $6 million expenditure limit, whereas high-revenue, asset-light software CCPCs should retain the default taxable capital test. Second, hardware, manufacturing, biotechnology, and AI companies acquiring depreciable equipment or GPUs on or after December 16, 2024, must implement operating-time logs to substantiate either the 90% All or Substantially All (ASA) threshold on Line 390 (ensuring those assets are excluded from T2 Schedule 8 CCA pools) or the >50% Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) threshold on Line 504, while software claimants must strictly segregate R&D cloud accounts from commercial production environments.

Third, claimants in Ontario, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba operating in a tax loss position should evaluate renouncing non-refundable provincial credits (such as the 3.5% Ontario ORDTC) by their T2 filing due date so those unutilized credits do not reduce their 35% refundable federal ITC base under Subsection 127(18), while Québec claimants should align their accounting systems with the unified R&D and pre-commercialisation (CRIC) rules for fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025. Fourth, because the Federal Court of Appeal in Kam-Press (2021 FCA 88) and National R&D (2022 FCA 72) confirmed that the Northwest Hydraulic five-part test—including adherence to the scientific method and contemporaneous documentation—remains binding law regardless of the CRA's 2021 Guidelines, engineering teams must record hypotheses, test metrics, and logical conclusions contemporaneously as the work progresses. Finally, claimants should utilize the CRA's 2026 elective Pre-Claim Approval Process to halve expenditure review times from 180 days to 90 days and enforce internal filing protocols well ahead of the non-discretionary 18-month statutory deadline across federal CRA, Revenu Québec, and Alberta TRA filings.
